appraisal_events.evidence: "je venais d'adresser à Albertine les paroles les plus dures et les plus humiliantes"; Rosemonde remarks to the narrator, "autrefois il n'y en avait que pour elle, c'était elle qui tenait la corde, maintenant elle n'est plus bonne à donner à manger aux chiens"; the narrator notices her hidden tears "non sans en être réjoui."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's cruel words openly humiliate Albertine, and a companion, Rosemonde, explicitly registers her fall from being the clear favorite to being utterly discarded; the narrator's private pleasure at her hidden tears underscores his emotional command of the scene.

appraisal_events.evidence: "j'étais en train, pour faire ressortir davantage encore mon attitude à l'égard d'Albertine, d'adresser toutes les amabilités possibles à Andrée qui... me semblait plus excusable."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator deliberately showers Andrée with kindness specifically to sharpen the contrast with his cruelty toward Albertine, a comparative, if calculated, elevation of Andrée in the same moment.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Celle-ci, qui se montrait glaciale avec les petits nobliaux que le voisinage de Féterne la forçait à fréquenter... me tendit au contraire la main avec un sourire rayonnant... très lié avec les Guermantes"; she sharply corrects her mother-in-law's modesty about the family's lineage ("Comment, pas illustre?... Tout un vitrail de la cathédrale de Bayeux...") and "déplorait son amabilité, craignant toujours que les gens n'eussent pas une idée suffisante des Cambremer."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator exposes Mme de Cambremer's glacial treatment of local nobility versus her radiant warmth toward anyone linked to the Guermantes, and her anxious policing of the family's prestige against her mother-in-law's modesty, revealing the same snobbish dependence on aristocratic regard already exposed in her brother Legrandin.

status_effects.explanation: She is openly humiliated and reduced to hidden tears while the narrator takes visible pleasure in her suffering, a clear loss of emotional ground.
Rosemonde's remark is a witnessed, third-party registration that Albertine has fallen from being unambiguously favored to being treated as worthless.
The narrator singles her out for kindness and finds her more excusable, a modest but real local elevation, even though the motive is tactical rather than sincere.

Her contrasting coldness toward local nobility and warmth toward a Guermantes-linked acquaintance, plus her anxious correction of her mother-in-law, expose a snobbish dependence on aristocratic prestige.
Her visible anxiety about the family's reputation, displayed in front of the assembled group, marks a witnessed dependence on others' regard rather than a secure standing of her own.
